3. Mr. Amirul Islam, the learned Counsel who appeared on behalf of the petitioner, has submitted that in this case, investigation was not completed within 180 days as provided under section 5A of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 and, as such, the investigation in this case should have been stopped and the accused persons released. In this connection, he has submitted that section 5 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act was amended by inserting section 5A by giving reference to the provisions of sub-section (5) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. According to him, this amendment was only with regard to the time limit for investigation and the newly added section provided for the time limit for investigation upto one hundred eighty days instead of sixty days as provided in sub-section (5) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. He further has argued that when there is any legislation by incorporation or by reference to any provision of law the application of the provision amended or added by such legislation be restricted to the extent of the reference made. He has also submitted that by the added section 5A, only the time limit for investigation is extended to 180 days in place of sixty days as provided under sub-section (5) of section 167 of Code of Criminal Procedure So, according to him, further amendment of sub-section (5) of section 167 by Act XLII of 1992 shall not affect the provisions of section 5A of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. 

 4. To give decision on the question raised by Mr. Amirul Islam, it is necessary to reproduce the relevant provisions of the law. The provisions are section 5A of Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958, Sub-sections (5) (6) and (7 A) of section 167 of Code of Criminal Procedure as those stood before 1992 and stood after amendment in 1992. Section 5A of Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 is as follows: 

 Provided that the Government may, by order, revive the case at any time if the case is triable exclusively by Court of Sessions)" 

 5. Section 5A was inserted in the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 in 1987 by Act XIII of 1987. This section 5A was inserted after section 5 of the above Act. In the added section 5A it is provided that sub-section (5) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure shall have effect as if for the word "Sixty days" the words "One hundred and eighty days" were substituted. It is obvious from this insertion of section 5A that the intention of the legislature was to extend the time limit for investigation. In the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958, there is no special or separate provision for holding investigation. Under sub-section (6) of section 5 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 a special Judge, where he deems it necessary, may pass an order for investigation by any police officer. 

 6. Now, in the added section 5A it is provided that for the purpose of investigation of an offence triable under this Act, the offence shall be deemed to be an offence triable exclusively by a Court of Sessions. So, it is clearly provided in the newly added Section 5A, that for the purpose of investigation the offence shall be deemed to be an offence triable by a Court of Sessions. In 1987, when this new section was added, time limit for investigation of any offence triable by the Court of sessions was sixty days under sub-section (5) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The legislature considered this time limit of sixty days to be inadequate for the purpose of investigation of offences triable by a Special Judge and, as such, 'by giving reference to sub-section (5) of section 167 of Code of Criminal Procedure, section 5A was added in the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 and the period of investigation was fixed as "one hundred eighty days", instead of "sixty days". 

 8. Mr. Islam has argued that as section 5A of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1958 was not amended after the amendment of sub-section (5) of section 167 of Code of Criminal Procedure in the year 1992, the amended provision of that sub-section (5) shall not be applicable in the present case but the earlier provision shall be applicable. We regret that we cannot accept this view. We have earlier noticed that there is no special and separate provision for holding investigation of a case under Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958. We have also noticed that for the purpose of investigation, offences of this Act shall be deemed to be offence triable by the Court of Sessions. So, the provisions of section 167 Code of Criminal Procedure shall apply in respect of investigation of the offences of the above Act and as regards the time limit for investigation, the same shall be one hundred eighty days instead of one hundred twenty days as provided in the amended sub-section (5) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. After the amendment of the provisions of sub- section (5) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in 1992 there is no scope of stopping the investigation on the ground of expiry of time limit specified for investigation. This position is equally true in respect of a Sessions case and a Special case. So, we are of the view that there was no necessity of amendment of section 5A of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 after amendment of the provisions of sub-section (5) of section 167 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in 1992. 

 It is true that under section 5A of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, investigation shall be held by an officer not below the rank of Inspector of Police. But as regards investigation of offences relating to corruption, a separate Bureau of Anti-Corruption was constituted under sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957. Under sub-sections (2) and (3) of section 3 of the above Act, the officers of the Bureau are empowered to hold investigation in respect of any offence specified in the schedule to that Act and offence notified by the Government. In the schedule to this Act at paragraph (B), offences punishable under the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 have been included. So, if we consider the provisions of section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 which is a later Act it cannot be said that investigation held by an Inspector of Bureau of Anti-Corruption was illegal because such Dower of investigation by an officer of the Bureau of Anti-Corruption has been given under section 3 of the above Act of 1957. However, if investigation is held by a police officer, such officer shall not be below the rank of an Inspector of Police in view of the provisions of section 5A of Act II of 1947. But when the investigation is held by any officer of Bureau of Anti-Corruption, in that case the provisions of section 5A of Act II of 1947 shall not be applicable but provisions of section 3 of the Anti-Corruption Act, 1957 shall apply. Moreover, in view of the provisions of para 59 of the Anti- corruption Manual, an officer of the Bureau is legally entitled to hold an investigation. So, in the instant case before us, no illegality was committed regarding holding of investigation in the case by an Inspector of Bureau of Anti-Corruption.
